data.title: Moment Group's (STO:MOMENT) Performance Raises Some Questions
data.description:
Moment Group AB (publ) (STO:MOMENT) recently released a strong earnings report, and the market responded by raising the share price. Despite the strong profit numbers, we believe that there are some deeper issues which investors should look into.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Examining Cashflow Against Moment Group's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

For the year to September 2026, Moment Group had an accrual ratio of 1.03. As a general rule, that bodes poorly for future profitability. To wit, the company did not generate one whit of free cashflow in that time. Even though it reported a profit of kr34.7m, a look at free cash flow indicates it actually burnt through kr19m in the last year. It's worth noting that Moment Group generated positive FCF of kr85m a year ago, so at least they've done it in the past. Having said that, there is more to the story. The accrual ratio is reflecting the impact of unusual items on statutory profit, at least in part. One positive for Moment Group shareholders is that it's accrual ratio was significantly better last year, providing reason to believe that it may return to stronger cash conversion in the future. Shareholders should look for improved cashflow relative to profit in the current year, if that is indeed the case.

See our latest analysis for Moment Group

Note: we always recommend investors check balance sheet strength. Click here to be taken to our balance sheet analysis of Moment Group.

The Impact Of Unusual Items On Profit

The fact that the company had unusual items boosting profit by kr2.1m, in the last year, probably goes some way to explain why its accrual ratio was so weak. While it's always nice to have higher profit, a large contribution from unusual items sometimes dampens our enthusiasm. When we analysed the vast majority of listed companies worldwide, we found that significant unusual items are often not repeated. And, after all, that's exactly what the accounting terminology implies. Assuming those unusual items don't show up again in the current year, we'd thus expect profit to be weaker next year (in the absence of business growth, that is).

Our Take On Moment Group's Profit Performance

Moment Group had a weak accrual ratio, but its profit did receive a boost from unusual items. For the reasons mentioned above, we think that a perfunctory glance at Moment Group's statutory profits might make it look better than it really is on an underlying level. data.title: How Fatal Ride Accident At Six Flags Entertainment (FUN) Has Changed Its Investment Story
data.description:
• Six Flags Entertainment reported third quarter 2026 revenue of US$195.55 million and a net loss of US$366.12 million, while also appointing experienced procurement leader Adam Boal as chief procurement officer and facing a legal investigation after a fatal roller coaster accident that led to nine ride closures.
  • The combination of continued operating losses, a new procurement executive focused on large scale spending and supplier management, and heightened safety scrutiny points to pressure on Six Flags Entertainment to control costs, manage risk, and maintain park operations under closer public and legal attention.
  • This article examines how Six Flags Entertainment's investment narrative is affected by the accident-driven safety review and the related legal investigation.

Six Flags Entertainment Investment Narrative Recap

To own Six Flags Entertainment today, you need to believe the park portfolio can produce enough cash to service its debt and still leave value for equity holders. The recent fatal accident, ride closures and securities investigation push safety, legal exposure and guest sentiment into the foreground. For now, the biggest near term swing factor is how quickly attendance and in park spending settle after this shock.

The largest risk remains the combination of operating losses, high leverage and negative shareholders' equity. Third quarter revenue of US$195.55 million and a net loss of US$366.12 million keep the focus on cash generation rather than headline valuation. According to FRAGMENTS, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, any asset sale or takeover thesis only works if the remaining parks support their own capital needs and debt costs.

The most relevant announcement here is the appointment of Adam Boal as chief procurement officer. His background at CBRE and AstraZeneca involved overseeing multi billion dollar spend, supplier platforms and third party risk. For Six Flags Entertainment, that experience sits right where investors are watching most closely: large capital projects, ride maintenance and safety critical vendors.

FRAGMENTS argues that park level cash flow and required investment already needed tighter scrutiny before the accident. Boal's role now links directly to that question: how to manage US$4.9b of net debt, substantial capital budgets and ongoing safety measures without eroding the value of flagship destinations. Execution on procurement discipline, rather than headlines about potential buyers, is likely to drive the next set of meaningful catalysts.

FRAGMENTS anchors a US$7.00 per share fair value on current operating cash flow, which does not independently support the more optimistic property valuations. The analysis still assigns some weight to the possibility of asset transactions and an improvement in Six Flags Entertainment's operations over time.

Exploring Other Perspectives

That is a much more pessimistic path than FRAGMENTS uses. data.title: Popular (BPOP) Declares Preferred Payouts As Its Valuation Gap Draws Attention
data.description:
Popular (BPOP) just declared a fresh round of income payments on its preferred and trust preferred securities, a small but concrete event that income focused investors tend to watch closely.

Those preferred payouts land at a time when Popular’s common shares have cooled from recent highs, with the share price down about 11% over the past three months but still showing a 25.3% year to date share price return and a 40.7% total shareholder return over the past year, which suggests that long term momentum has been stronger than the latest pullback.

Scan beyond Popular’s latest preferred payouts and recent share pullback to see how it compares with a curated 32 high quality undervalued stocks that also pair income potential with balance sheet strength.

After an 11% pullback and with Popular changing hands below both analyst targets and intrinsic value estimates, the gap between price and fair value looks wide enough to measure. How far off are those curves?

Price-to-Earnings of 9.9x: Is it justified?

Popular’s valuation picture starts with a simple anchor. At a last close of $157.88, the stock trades on a P/E of 9.9x that screens as good value against both peers and broader US banks.

The P/E ratio compares what investors are paying today for each dollar of Popular’s earnings. For a lender with a long operating history, earnings quality matters as much as the headline multiple, and here the business scores firmly in the “high quality earnings” bucket, with current net profit margins of 32.2% versus 27% a year earlier.

That gap between price and earnings power is reinforced in two ways. First, the P/E of 9.9x sits below the US Banks industry average of 11.3x and below a peer group average of 12.7x. This suggests the market is assigning a discount relative to comparable institutions. Second, the estimated fair P/E for Popular is 11.8x. This is a level the market could move toward if sentiment around its earnings profile and 2.28% dividend support were to align more closely with sector norms.
